title: Nested Text Analysis
text:
Summary
The boxplot definitely back up Susan Easton Black’s quote, showing that the median distance between mentions of the Savior stays consistently low—around 25 to 50 words—across almost every single book. You can clearly see how the narrative style affects the spacing, books heavy on history or conflict like Helaman have wider boxes, while Alma is absolutely packed with outliers stretching all the way to the 300-word limit. On the flip side, books like Moroni and Mormon have super tight distributions, meaning the references to Christ are packed very closely together. Overall, despite the long tails from some of the story heavy sections, the graph proves His name is constantly woven throughout the entire text.

AI USAGE
Helped me to used fct_rev(book_title) on the y-axis of the plot. By default, ggplot builds the y-axis from the bottom up, which would put 1 Nephi at the bottom. Reversing it ensures 1 Nephi is at the top, making it read naturally from top to bottom. Copilot helped me write the analysis too.

title: Costa Rica Species Map
text:
Summary
Since I am from Costa Rica I really wanted to map something related to my home country so I pulled live spatial data from the GBIF database to map 2000 recent sightings each for two famous animals: Brown-throated Sloths and White-faced Capuchin Monkeys. To build the map I just combined a polygon layer for the subtle provincial boundaries with a point layer (the circle markers) for the actual animal sightings. I chose a topographic basemap because it clearly shows the mountain ranges and coastlines, which naturally affect where these animals live. To make the map easy to read and interactive, I color-coded the sloths green and the monkeys orange, and added a layer control box in the top right corner so users can toggle the animals on and off to compare their habitats.
Playing with the toggles shows some really interesting ecological patterns. The capuchin monkeys are basically everywhere, they have a super widespread distribution all along both coasts and cluster heavily around major national parks like Manuel Antonio, showing just how adaptable they are. The sloth data on the other hand, tells a different story. You can clearly see a massive concentration of sloths in the northern plains and along the humid Caribbean coast in Limón, but there is a huge empty spot in the northwest province of Guanacaste. Since Guanacaste is famous for its dry tropical forests it perfectly visualizes how sloths much prefer the wetter, more humid rainforests found in the rest of the country, kinda cool!

Questions

Which origin airport is best to minimize my chances of a late arrival when I am using Delta Airlines?


Code
deltaFlights <- flights %>%
  filter(carrier == "DL", !is.na(arr_delay))

ggplot(deltaFlights, aes(x = origin, y = arr_delay, color = origin)) +
  geom_jitter(alpha = 0.1, width = 0.2) + 
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Arrival Delays for Delta Airlines by Origin", subtitle = "Individual flights shown to highlight variability", x = "Origin Airport", y = "Arrival Delay (minutes)") +
  theme_minimal()









Based on the data, LGA (LaGuardia) is the best origin for Delta passengers. Though all three airports show a high density of flights arriving early (below the 0-minute line), LGA has a tighter distribution of delays and a lower average arrival delay (\(3.47\) minutes) compared to JFK (\(5.55\) minutes) and EWR (\(12.1\) minutes). If you want to avoid significant “outlier” delays, LGA provides the most consistent performance for Delta. I dind’t normalized the data, due to insufficient data.


Which destination airport is the worst airport for arrival delays? You decide on the metric for “worst.”
For this graph/analysis, I have defined “worst” as the highest average arrival delay (since it sucks being late), considering only airports that received at least 100 flights to ensure the sample size is meaningful and keep it normalized. This avoids skewing results with a single, highly delayed flight to a rare destination.


Code
worstDests <- flights %>%
  filter(!is.na(arr_delay)) %>%
  group_by(dest) %>%
  summarize( avg_delay = mean(arr_delay), flight_count = n()) %>%
  filter(flight_count >= 100) %>%
  arrange(desc(avg_delay)) %>%
  head(10)

ggplot(worstDests, aes(x = reorder(dest, avg_delay), y = avg_delay, fill = avg_delay)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "orange", high = "darkred") +
  labs(title = "Top 10 Worst Destination Airports", subtitle = "By Average Arrival Delay (Min. 100 flights)", x = "Destination Airport Code", y = "Average Arrival Delay (minutes)") +
  theme_minimal()









The worst destination airport for arrival delays is CAE (Columbia Metropolitan Airport) in South Carolina, with an average arrival delay of approximately 25.9 minutes. It is closely followed by TUL (Tulsa) and OKC (Oklahoma City). This suggests that flights heading to these specific regional hubs from NYC are significantly more likely to face arrival bottlenecks or scheduling issues compared to major hubs like ATL or LAX.

title: Combining Height Datasets
text:
4 (How did I tidy it up?)
To get all these datasets playing nicely together I had to wrangle five totally different file formats (.csv, .dta, .sav, and .dbf) into one clean master dataset. I actually leaned on Gemini to help speed up writing the dplyr logic, which was a huge timesaver! The biggest hurdle was standardizing the units, like the historical German datasets used centimeters, while the modern US ones used inches (or a messy mix of feet and inches). To fix that I just calculated standard height.in and height.cm columns across the board. I also had to make a few hard calls on what data to drop. For the BLS set I filtered out the female participants to keep things apples-to-apples with the male-only German soldier and prisoner records. Finanlly, I scrubbed the Wisconsin survey to drop anyone who answered ‘-1’ or ‘-2’ (‘Refused’ or ‘Don’t Know’), because if I hadn’t caught that, those negative numbers would have completely wrecked the height conversions and skewed the rest of the analysis. After all that, I used bind_rows to stitch everything together into one big tidy dataset.

# chronological order of the studies using factors (c())

  mutate(study = factor(study, levels = c(
    "German Soldiers",       # 18th Century
    "Bavarian Prisoners",    # 19th Century
    "Bavarian Conscripts",   # 19th Century
    "BLS Height Data",       # Mid-20th Century
    "Wisconsin Survey"       # Late 20th/21st Century
  )))

# realistic human heights 
allHeights_filtered <- allHeights %>%
  filter(height.in >= 48 & height.in <= 90)

ggplot(allHeights_filtered, aes(x = study, y = height.in, fill = study)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.alpha = 0.3) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Heights Across Centuries",subtitle = "Comparing 18th/19th century German records to modern US surveys", x = "Study (Chronological Order)", y = "Height (Inches)") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1), legend.position = "none" )

title: Combining Height Datasets
text:
6
When you look at the plot I just generated, the story it tells seems pretty straightforward at first, but then it throws a massive curveball that seems to contradict everything. If you just look at the progression from the 18th and 19th-century German records to the mid-20th-century BLS data, the median height clearly trends upward, jumping from around 65-67 inches to about 70 inches. But then we hit the Wisconsin Survey data from the late 20th century, and the median suddenly tanks back down to around 66 inches, contradicting the whole “up-and-to-the-right” growth trend. If you were just glancing at the chart, you’d think humans peaked in the 1950s and then started shrinking. But the contradiction makes perfect sense when you look under the hood at the data dictionary. The German military/prison records and the BLS dataset we filtered were strictly male-only samples. The Wisconsin survey, however, didn’t have a gender identifier, meaning it’s a mix of both men and women. Because women have a lower average height, throwing them into the dataset naturally drags the median down and widens the overall spread of the boxplot.
So, if someone asserted that “humans are getting taller over time” based strictly on these datasets, I’d tell them they are technically right, but their data hygiene is a little sloppy. You can clearly see the historical growth trend when comparing the historic male-only datasets to the modern male-only BLS dataset as nutrition, medicine, and living conditions improved over the centuries, average heights went up. But you simply can’t use the Wisconsin survey to prove or disprove that specific trend because it’s an apples-to-oranges comparison. Overall, my stance is that while the data absolutely supports the idea that human height increased over the last few hundred years, this whole exercise is a massive warning about why you can’t just blindly bind_rows() on random datasets and trust the visualization without understanding exactly who is in your sample.
(Shoutout to Gemini for helping me debug the R code, figure out the missing variables, and wrangle these messy datasets into shape to build out this analysis!)

title: Building Footprints by State
text:
Summary
The data shows exactly how bad the 2007–2010 housing collapse really was. It wasn’t just big cities that got hit; it happened everywhere. If you look at the US map, almost every state saw a massive drop in single-family building permits starting around 2006. We see the exact same thing right here in Idaho. It didn’t matter if it was a fast-growing place like Ada and Canyon counties or smaller, outdoor-focused spots like Valley and Blaine counties building permits just completely fell off a cliff when the crash started. Building permits are a good early warning sign for the economy. These charts show that new housing basically froze everywhere, often way before regular people really felt the effects of the 2008 financial crisis
To show these trends honestly, I designed the graphics to focus on the shape of the crash rather than the raw numbers. The biggest challenge with this kind of data is the huge difference in scale. For example, if we put California and North Dakota on the exact same scale, California’s massive numbers would make North Dakota’s line look completely flat and hide their local crash. By letting each state and county have its own vertical scale, it’s way easier to focus on when the boom and bust happened. Also, laying out the national data to look like a US map makes it super easy to spot regional patterns, so anyone can quickly find and understand what happened in their specific area

title: Open Data Source Evaluation

Here are 4 potential free data sources I explored for this project, along with an assessment of their general quality:

Data.gov: The official US government open data portal.

Quality: Highly authoritative but heavily variable in structure. Datasets often require extensive cleaning and formatting, and metadata can sometimes be sparse.

Kaggle Datasets: A community-driven platform for data science.

Quality: Highly variable. Some datasets are pristine and meticulously documented by organizations, while others are uploaded by users with no data dictionary, missing values, and unverified sources.

World Bank Open Data: Global economic, demographic, and health data.

Quality: Excellent. The data is rigorously standardized and heavily documented, though you will often encounter missing values for certain developing nations or specific years.

TidyTuesday Project: A weekly social data project in R.

Quality: Very good. The data is pre-curated to be interesting and accessible, but it is deliberately left slightly “messy” so users can practice their data wrangling skills.

title: Open Data Source Evaluation
text:
Limitations
While this dataset is high quality it has limitations in addressing my original question like
Geographic Scope: It only covers three islands in the Palmer Archipelago. We cannot extrapolate these findings to penguin populations in Antarctica at large or in other regions of the world.
Temporal Scope: The data was collected between 2007 and 2009. It does not allow us to see long-term trends, such as how climate change might be affecting body mass over decades, but that’s ok by me

library(tidyverse)

url <- "https://byuistats.github.io/M335/data/chipotle_reduced.csv"

# parse the JSON dictionary string into a tibble
extract_visits <- function(json_str) {
  if (is.na(json_str) || json_str == "") return(tibble(day = character(), visits = numeric()))
  
  parsed <- fromJSON(json_str)
  tibble(
    day = names(parsed),
    visits = as.numeric(parsed)
  )
}

# each row using map to create a nested list column
chipotle_nested <- chipotle_raw |>
  mutate(daily_visits = map(popularity_by_day, extract_visits))




2


Code
chipotle_unnested <- chipotle_nested |>
  unnest(daily_visits) |>
  # chronologically 
  mutate(day = factor(day, levels = c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday")))

total_visits_df <- chipotle_unnested |>
  group_by(day) |>
  summarize(total_visits = sum(visits, na.rm = TRUE))

ggplot(total_visits_df, aes(x = day, y = total_visits)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#8C1515") + 
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +

  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16))









In this newly created chipotle_unnested dataset a single observation represents the total number of visits for one specific day of the week at one specific Chipotle location.


3


Code
busiest_day_df <- chipotle_unnested |>
  group_by(placekey) |>
  slice_max(order_by = visits, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup()

peak_store_counts <- busiest_day_df |>
  count(day, name = "store_count") |>
  # all days are represented even if count is 0
  complete(day, fill = list(store_count = 0))

ggplot(peak_store_counts, aes(x = day, y = store_count)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#E7711B") + 
  theme_minimal() +
  geom_text(aes(label = store_count), vjust = -0.5, fontface = "bold", color = "gray30") +
  labs(title = "Most Common Busiest Days for Chipotle Locations", x = NULL, y = "Number of Restaurants") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16))









In the busiest_day_df dataset an observation represents a single Chipotle restaurant and the specific day of the week that it experiences its highest visitor count.


Recommendations
I definitely recommend running this big promotion on a Friday. If leadership is leaning toward a two-day event, a Thursday-Friday combination is absolutely the way to go.
While both visualizations point to the end of the workweek as the peak time, the graph showing the Most Common Busiest Days for Chipotle Locations (the store count) was by far the most influential in making this call. Looking at total visits alone can be a bit deceiving because a handful of massive, high volume flagship stores or locations near big events can heavily skew those aggregate numbers. By looking at the count of individual restaurants instead, we get a much clearer picture of what the typical, average location is actually experiencing. For 965 distinct locations, Friday is their absolute busiest day, and Thursday is a solid runner-up with 704 locations peaking. This metric ensures the promotion actually aligns with the peak operational rush for the vast majority of our teams on the ground, rather than just catering to the chain’s heaviest hitters.
A couple of other interesting insights stood out in the data, too:

The “Taco Tuesday” Effect: There is a noticeable, distinct spike in traffic on Tuesdays compared to both Mondays and Wednesdays. It looks like that cultural mindset brings a small but reliable mid-week boost to the stores.
The Sunday Slump: Sunday is universally the slowest day across the board—only 25 locations consider it their peak day. While the current goal is to run the promo when it’s busiest, if leadership ever pivots and wants to use a promotion to drive traffic and balance labor on dead days, Sunday would be the obvious target.
